# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Gets Upstairs

Water is heavy. A single cubic meter of it weighs a thousand kilograms, and a typical city moves millions of those cubic meters every day, often lifting a substantial fraction of it tens or hundreds of meters into the air. The remarkable thing is that when you turn on a shower on the 30th floor, water arrives instantly, at a predictable pressure, without anyone having thought about it. Understanding how that happens requires a tour through gravity, hydraulics, and a surprising amount of deliberate engineering slack.

## The Fundamental Problem: Elevation and Head

The core physics is simple. Water pressure in a static column is purely a function of height. Every 10 meters of elevation costs you roughly one atmosphere of pressure, or about 14.7 pounds per square inch. Engineers call this "head" — the vertical distance water must be lifted, expressed in pressure terms. To deliver usable water at a faucet, you need not just enough head to reach the tap, but a surplus — typically 20 to 30 PSI — so that water flows out with reasonable force rather than dribbling.
